prize_parts.citation: for showing how firm heterogeneity, selection into exporting and reallocation across firms shape the gains from trade

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1, but I am clearer about why. In my opening I ranked B001 first. I moved to B048 because B048 has the stronger evidentiary record. Melitz (2003) and the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple extensions gave trade a mechanism, selection into exporting and reallocation across firms, together with a structure that firm-level and customs data could test. Over twenty years and many countries, the qualitative predictions (exporter premia, selection, within-industry reallocation after liberalisation) have largely held. I weigh most heavily the combination of a new explanatory framework with new empirical data. B048 has that, and its core claims have been exposed to repeated testing. The attribution is also tighter: the central model and its main extension sit with two named people, so the three-name cap costs little. The chair's summary shows B048 and B001 as the main contest. After the exchange I still put B048 ahead, though the gap is not large and I treat it as a judgement about robustness, not a verdict on importance. Nothing in round 1 argued that field rotation or the 2008 prize is evidence about merit, and I do not rely on either.
statement.case_against: The main risk is priority. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum developed closely parallel firm-level facts and models, and they are not on this ballot entry. A two-name credit could be read as favouring the theory over the empirical foundations, and the three-name cap cannot fix that. Welfare-gain magnitudes depend on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity, so the citation should not claim more than the mechanism. Helpman also appears in the B026 trade-politics package, which blurs his claim at the margin. Redding's quantitative and spatial work is a later strand that this credit leaves out by design. Finally, my own preference for identification-based arguments may tilt me toward candidates with clean empirical tests, and I should not overstate how decisive that criterion is.

responses.point: Hassler prefers B001 but calls the gap with B048 small. He would word the citation around measurable institutions and established regularities, not the strong causal legal-origins reading, and he accepts that excluding Vishny is a real attribution cost.
responses.response: I accept his drafting. A citation saying that legal institutions and investor protection can be measured across countries and co-vary systematically with financial outcomes is honest, and I would not call it an overclaim. It also changes what is being rewarded. The discovery becomes a body of empirical regularities and a research design, not an identified causal effect. That is a real contribution, but it is weaker than a mechanism whose predictions have survived micro-data tests. The cap still removes Vishny from the founding papers, and no wording fixes that. Under his citation, B001 stays my first alternative, and I think the remaining difference with B048 is about robustness, not importance.

responses.point: Friberg keeps B001 first with moderate confidence. He rests the case on the field-creating contribution and on 25 years of testing, and he concedes that B001 does not compete on identification strength. He lists B048 as his first alternative.
responses.response: I appreciate his candour about identification, because it narrows the disagreement to one question: whether field creation should outweigh how well the central claims have held. I count the critiques as evidence about maturity. The literature the work produced has qualified the headline mechanism, and a citation must say what was established. I do not dismiss field creation. If the committee judges that a prize should reward the question and the data it created, his ordering is defensible, and that is why B001 is my first alternative. Where we differ is that I would not let breadth of influence substitute for robustness once a cleaner candidate with tested predictions is available.

responses.point: Krusell prefers B037 (Kiyotaki, Moore, Gertler). He sees the collateral-constraint mechanism as a clean, mature, reusable idea. He lists B048 as his first alternative and would accept a two-name Kiyotaki-Moore version if Gertler's credit is judged too entangled with B040.
responses.response: I agree that Kiyotaki and Moore are an unambiguous core and that the mechanism has stayed intact for nearly thirty years. That is a strength of B037. My hesitation is the one he states himself: collateral channels are harder to identify empirically than the theory's influence suggests, and the 2022 overlap reduces the marginal case, even if it is not disqualifying. Gertler's credit is also split with B040. I would not use the 2022 prize as a merit argument against the theory. I would say that B048 is better corroborated by micro-data, and its credit divides more cleanly. I would not list B037 as an alternative only because the protocol limits me to two, and I would find a two-name version defensible.

responses.point: Strömberg prefers B001. He argues that the critiques qualify the mechanism more than the discovery, and that the cross-country regularities and the research agenda would survive even if legal origin is only partly causal. He names B048 and B049 as fallbacks if the committee wants a cleaner identification record.
responses.response: I agree that critiques of a mechanism do not erase a field. His distinction between the facts and the causal story is the strongest B001 argument I have heard in this exchange. It also tells me what the citation would honour: facts and a design, not an explanation. By the standard I use across fields, that makes B001 less complete than a candidate whose mechanism and facts both stand. I note that he himself names B048 as a fallback when identification matters. On his Vishny point, I agree the trio is defensible, but I do not think it is costless.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum priority question as material. I would draft the citation around the selection and reallocation mechanism and the gains-from-trade framework, which limits the exposure without removing it.
Whether Helpman's separate appearance on B026 should be handled by defining the B048 citation tightly or is an unresolved competing-claim issue. I lean toward tight definition.

How much weight to give B001's field-creating role relative to the contested causal reading. This is the main thing that could reverse my ordering, and it depends on how the committee weighs influence against robustness.
How sensitive the size of the selection gains is to functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity, and whether this should limit the wording of the citation.
Whether thematic overlap with recent prizes is a timing consideration only. I treat it as not bearing on scientific merit.
My assessments rely on my own knowledge of the literature and are not independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Melitz, Helpman, or the credited names on B001 or B015 is documented in my supplied profile. My listed frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not among them. My field is labour economics and the economics of crime, which is not the field of B048. The chair's summary notes a possible familiarity bias toward empirical-design arguments, and I confirm that disclosure: it may inflate how much I value identification and testability. My profile records editorial roles at economics journals and a prior committee year in which Goldin was awarded for work at the intersection of labour economics and economic history. I do not see these as candidate connections. I did not take them as grounds for recusal, and I do not adjudicate them. I claim no independent verification of any source.
